blocks.heading: Choosing work
blocks.text:
Occupational choice is an individual’s selection of a type of work, subject to preferences, opportunities and requirements. Earnings matter because they support spending and saving, but work also occupies time, affects safety and can provide interest, skills or satisfaction. Wage factors concern monetary earnings; non-wage factors concern other job characteristics. A person comparing jobs therefore needs more than the headline monthly pay. Required qualifications, available vacancies and the ability to reach a workplace also affect which choices are feasible.

An applicant may choose a nearby N$5,200 job over a N$5,700 job requiring unpredictable night shifts. The extra N$500 is a wage advantage, while the working pattern and location are non-wage considerations. The choice is not irrational merely because it does not maximise stated earnings. Its quality depends on the person’s needs, alternatives and costs. Another applicant may reasonably prefer the higher-paying role. No single ranking follows from these figures alone.

Changing occupation differs from changing location. Occupational mobility of labour is the ease with which workers can move from one type of job to another. Geographical mobility of labour is the ease with which workers can move from one area to another. Labour is occupationally immobile when it lacks the skills, qualifications or training for other work, and geographically immobile when moving is limited by housing costs, family or cultural ties, or lack of information about jobs elsewhere. Training that lets a clerk become a technician supports occupational mobility. Moving towns while continuing as a clerk concerns geographical mobility. A person can experience both changes, but they remain separate dimensions. This links to earnings in topic 4.2 and employment in topic 7.2: a wage difference does not prove workers can immediately change jobs, since skills and movement can constrain access.

People can also choose self-employment (working for themselves) instead of being an employee. Self-employment offers independence, flexible hours and keeping all the profit, but brings irregular income, long hours, responsibility for any losses and no paid leave or employer pension.
